note: MarketLab Terminal hosted-path inventory (FINCEPT_FORK_PLAN.md §5.3). Two sections, two checks, both enforced by audit_hosted_paths.py. "rules": every Fincept-owned host reference in src/, scripts/, resources/, packaging/, and translations/ must be listed with an explicit disposition. "sinks": every occurrence in the scanned sink scopes — under src/ for the C++/QML sinks, and in the reachable production Python under scripts/ for the Python sinks — of an API that can initiate outbound contact must be listed with an explicit disposition — this is the half of the control that can see a configuration-derived route, whose host never appears as a literal in the source and which therefore no host rule could ever catch. Either check fails when a new occurrence appears without a disposition. Dispositions (both sections): removed | guarded | unreachable | not_built | rejected | disabled. "sink_counts": the exact occurrence count of every (file, sink) pair, because a per-file disposition on its own rubber-stamps every FUTURE site in a file it already covers — a second connectToHost() added to a file already marked "guarded" would otherwise pass unseen.

sinks_note: Network-sink inventory. Sink kinds: tcp_socket (QTcpSocket / connectToHost), network_access_manager (any QNetworkAccessManager owned outside the shared HttpClient), websocket (QWebSocket), open_url (QDesktopServices::openUrl, ShellExecute, or a QProcess browser launch). C++ sink scope is src/ only — a sink in tests/ is not in the product. The Python sink scope (py_http_client, py_urllib, py_socket, py_websocket, py_sdk_client) is the transitive local-import closure of the .py entry points named as string literals in src/ — the Python children the application actually launches, which do their own networking inside the child process. Selectors are an exact path or a "dir/**" subtree; the "*" catch-all is rejected by the loader, because disposing of every present and future sink in one line is precisely the defect this section exists to remove. A subtree selector is used only where every file under it genuinely shares one disposition and one reason.

sinks.note: The fork's only four outbound connectToHost() probes: the Data Sources connection tester, the ds_test_connection MCP tool, the Data Sources live-status poller, and the data-source workflow node. Each takes host/port from a stored connector config — a configuration-derived route that no literal-host scan can see — and each applies HostedPathGuard before the socket: is_fincept_destination() on the URL form (which decides the path-scoped Fincept GitHub-org rules) and is_fincept_host() on the bare host+port form, returning the typed HOSTED_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE error with no connection attempted.

Inbound only: a QTcpServer bound to QHostAddress::LocalHost on an OS-assigned port, exposing the internal MCP tool catalog to the local Python agent subprocess. The QTcpSocket instances are connections Qt returns from nextPendingConnection(); there is no connectToHost() and no outbound destination. Every request is additionally gated by a constant-time X-MCP-Token compare and auth/LoopbackGuard.h.

The three clients that own their own QNetworkAccessManager, so the shared client's deny-list cannot see their requests. Each rejects for itself through network/http/DirectRouteGuard.h before the QNAM is touched: CloudClient::reject_hosted() on every get/post/put/del, QuantLibClient::call() on the configuration-derived api_base_url()+"/quantlib/" route, ArenaLlmClient::complete() on the resolved provider endpoint. Covered by tests/tst_direct_clients.cpp. alpha_arena is additionally not a registered screen.

DirectRouteGuard.h documents which clients own one; TerminalShell.h documents why bootstrap_auth() must run after the event loop exists; the two MCP files document why a tool handler running on a QtConcurrent worker must marshal onto the thread that owns the service's QNAM.

The status bar's QNetworkAccessManager member survives, but the Fincept API-health ping it existed for (GET api.fincept.in/health on a 30s timer) is removed: ping_api() now only sets local labels and issues no request, so the QNAM is constructed and never used.

Each of these owns its own QNetworkAccessManager and fetches a URL that comes from configuration — a user-typed scrape target, a stored or imported RSS feed, a workflow node parameter — so the shared HttpClient deny-list never sees the request and no literal host appears anywhere in the tree. They now construct network::GuardedNetworkAccessManager instead, whose createRequest() override refuses a Fincept-owned destination before any connection is made and returns an already-failed reply, so each caller reports it through the error path it already had (FINCEPT_FORK_PLAN.md §5.3). Every file in this rule now constructs the guarded manager, including the ones whose endpoint is a fixed third-party service (Deepgram, NewsAPI, OSM/Carto tiles): for those the guard is a no-op, and making the class uniform is what stops a later edit from reintroducing a raw manager next to a guarded one without anyone noticing.

Endpoints are resolved by ProviderCatalog, whose is_blocked() hard-refuses the removed hosted "fincept" provider and any base_url containing fincept.in / .com / .app / .ai; LlmService::endpoint_url() consults that block before it resolves anything, which is what makes its remaining p=="fincept" branch dead.

Opt-in cloud telemetry. Guarded, not merely off. The endpoint is the user's own telemetry.cloud_endpoint setting, so it is a configuration-derived route: no literal-host scan can see where it points, and §5.3 requires such a route to be contained rather than assumed safe because the feature defaults off. Two containments now apply. The manager is a GuardedNetworkAccessManager, so every request — and, since Qt does not re-enter createRequest() on a redirect, every redirect hop — is judged by HostedPathGuard before a connection is made. And read_config() refuses a Fincept-owned telemetry.cloud_endpoint outright, logging the refusal once per configuration and leaving the uploader idle; the chained LocalTelemetrySink still persists every event to disk. The earlier "disabled" disposition described the default, not the guarantee — an operator who set the endpoint to a Fincept host and flipped telemetry.cloud_enabled would have reached it.

sink_counts_note: Pinned occurrence count of every (file, sink) pair in the scanned sink scopes (under src/, and the reachable production Python under scripts/), exhaustive and exact. This is the half of the sink check that is keyed on the SITES rather than on the file: the dispositions above answer "is this judged?", these numbers answer "is this still the same set of sites that was judged?". A count that goes up is a new outbound-capable site and fails the audit even though its file (or its "dir/**" subtree) is already dispositioned; a count that goes down, or a file that disappears, also fails, so the inventory cannot drift away from the tree. Counts are textual occurrences of the sink regex, comments included — editing a comment that names QNetworkAccessManager will move a number, and that is the intended cost of pinning sites rather than files. Known limit: a change that adds one sink and deletes another of the same kind in the same file leaves the count equal and is not caught; site-level pinning is a different and much larger control.
